story_text.value:
I've seen too many slow-log queries with a GROUP BY that makes Postgres blow up, so for the last two weeks or so I've been working on Straum. You declare the aggregates as a view, and Straum answers over HTTP (other transports might be added). I've been using the New York taxi dataset as a benchmark. On the heavier GROUP BYs I see about 1,000x to 5,000x. It's written in Rust (of course).

It leans on Postgres replication slots, logical or physical, to get its data. Postgres stays the source of truth.

Benchmark: https://janbjorge.github.io/straum/benchmark.html Repo: https://github.com/janbjorge/straum

title.value: Show HN: Straum – a Postgres materialized view that is never stale

story_text.value:
Hey HN, I made Peek, a Mac app for quickly checking the things you check often without switching apps.

You just need to hold the hotkey ( Fn by default) to bring up the websites and widgets you need in a layer over what you're doing. Release it and you're back. To interact with the contents inside, you just tap the hotkey to keep it open.

The idea came from FPS/MOBA/... games: you hold a key to check the scoreboard or map, then release it to get back to playing. I wanted that same quick interaction for the things I check while working.

Personally, I keep calendar widget, reminders widget and X feed for my Peek zone.

And few other things Peek can do:

- Add websites, local PDF and HTML files to Peek

- Built-in widgets: timezones, weather, stocks

- MCP: let your agents make custom widgets and add them to Peek

- Hide unwanted elements of a webpage

- Auto-refresh webpages

- Work over full-screen apps

- Use separate layouts for different displays

Peek is a one-time purchase, currently available at an early believer price of $3.99.

I’d love to hear what you’d keep in your Peek zone :)

I also made a launch video on YouTube: https://youtu.be/yziiGo_Hq6Q

story_text.value:
I am ashamed to admit that I am one of those students who go to the library and get very little done (a.k.a. larping). It's very easy to get distracted if you have any electronic devices with you, but as a CS major, I can't just switch to pen and paper. That's why I started building this app called LarpLess with the help of a few friends.

LarpLess is a macOS/Windows app that checks your screen and camera with local AI to determine what you are studying or if you are distracted. Gives you a focus percentage at the end, with a breakdown of what you did during your session (Math, Physics, etc.)

Privacy is a big concern for an app like this, so it is open-source (AGPL 3.0) and uses locally run open-source models. It doesn't connect to the internet unless you want to check for updates or enable the friends feature (Disabled by default. You can make an account, add friends and see their shared study sessions/share your study sessions).

For the camera, it uses an object detection model, YOLO11n, to detect if there is a person and/or a phone at 1fps. For the screen, there are 2 options: the one we did first is reading window titles + a VLM on Ollama (default is qwen3-vl:2b), simple but power/RAM hungry. The one my friend added later can run on an average laptop easily. It takes less than a second for a verdict. It scores window titles + OCR text on the screen with MiniLM text embeddings and scores the screenshot with image embeddings using SigLIP 2. SigLIP 2 decides if the user is distracted, and MiniLM decides what they are working on. You can run the classifier-based mode on any modern laptop. If you want to use the VLM mode, you need a good GPU with enough VRAM (3GB+) to hold the model in it.

You can try it out by downloading the macOS version from GitHub (https://github.com/AlperErg/larpless/releases) or the Windows version from the Microsoft Store (https://apps.microsoft.com/detail/9nrvvphtmr9x).

I found it helpful for studying. I hope that you will as well. I'd appreciate it if you can give it a go and kindly share your thoughts.

p.s. My friend, who also works on this with me, posted about it before but without a description and not on Show HN, so I decided to post on Show HN with a good description.

title.value: Show HN: LarpLess, open-source study tracker detecting distractions locally

story_text.value:
Hello! I'm Marc.

I've built "Nunya", which is a sort of "digital privacy screen".

It redraws text to make it readable when looking at your monitor or phone from a normal distance, while making it hard to read by someone who might be looking over your shoulder.

It's based on “hybrid images” like the famous Einstein/Monroe image (from the paper at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1141911.1141919) and I thought it'd make a great way to mask text on your phone that you don't want someone nearby reading.

I particularly spent time on the transition - I wanted the text to be incredibly legible when close, but incredibly illegible when being far, and tried to optimise for a minimal transition between the two.

Demos can be seen at my site for it here: https://usenunya.com

I first released this over ten years ago as "PrivacyMessage" (my app names have definitely improved) when Apple first allowed iMessage apps. This was my first app geared towards the general market as I've spent the last 13 years developing iOS apps for a fairly niche market.

I'm happy to have brought it back as “Nunya”, and have currently made it available in three forms:

- Nunya for Messages (iPhone)

I first remade my iMessage app and gave it a bit more polish. It's free for 5 sends, and then $4.99 for a permanent unlock.

- Potfolio (iPhone)

I then figured Nunya would make for a great flagship feature in a "wealth tracking" finance app I was already working on, so anyone who might glance at your phone when on public transport can't quite see your bank balances. It's currently free (though I might add some new features with IAPs to it later).

- Nunya for Chrome

A friend then suggested it'd make for a great Chrome extension to be used on all sites. It's free to hide money amounts, and £10 (around $13) to unlock it to work with more (bank details, bitcoin addresses, etc). You can try it here: https://usenunya.com/chrome

This is my first real attempt at making apps for a wider market. It's also my very first Chrome extension, and I'm not entirely sure how best to price each of these, nor how to best gate their features. I don't particularly like subscriptions if I can avoid them.

I'm curious to hear any thoughts. Particularly: do you think these pricing models are reasonable? I also wonder if Nunya would make for a good feature elsewhere. With more staff working remotely who might be in transit or in cafes, I can imagine businesses could be keen for their staff to use it on more sensitive data. Does that seem plausible?

Thanks all.

title.value: Show HN: Nunya – A "digital privacy screen" that makes text illegible from afar

story_text.value:
Hello!

One of my hobbies is curling in a league with the local curling club. From time to time, there's a setup of stones that is tricky and interesting to contemplate from a strategic perspective. A while back, I started working on a three.js-based curling simulator that would enable me to recreate situations from my league games and then try different shots.

As you may know, curling is notoriously tricky from a physics perspective. There are a variety of papers out there about this, including this one, which is one of the more recent dives into understanding why stones curl the way they do: https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-018-26595-y

Anyhow, with the help of Claude Code, I pulled together the work and converted the quick-and-dirty sim into a game you can play online. It's still a bit more of a sim than a game, perhaps, but it can be fun to play as a game.

Curling often is referred to as "chess on ice" because there's more strategy in choosing shots and playing ends than there would appear to be at first glance. The primary challenge of turning this into a game has been trying to figure out how to provide the computer player both with a policy for game and end-level strategy while also having it evaluate the tactical choices that have to be made for each shot.

For example, when would the computer try to blank (no points scored) an end deliberately so that it can retain hammer (last stone thrown) in the subsequent end? When should it throw a low vs. high center or corner guard in an attempt to make up a point deficit? When should it try to steal points from the hammer team vs. throwing protective stones that hold the hammer team to one point?

It's a fun side project for me, so I thought you all might enjoy giving it a shot. :)

p.s. In a game, if you go into the settings, you can turn on debug mode, which will reveal a panel on the right with a variety of (currently-undocumented) parameters you can tweak.

formbook is a horse racing analytics app im building with model odds and stats, im a few weeks away from going live with the full app but im hosting the mcp open right now for testing so you can plug your agent into all the data

  claude mcp add --transport http --scope user formbook https://mcp.formbook.io/mcp
the data is about 30 years worth, full coeverage uk/ire, most of hong kong and dubai, major races from most major racing regions with sectionals and stride date from last few years

the mcp gives you access to upcoming racecards and the model's prices/confidence, live bookmaker odds and delayed exchange odds

its currently running on my recently nerfed oracle free tier server so performance will be worse than production but agent working time is the biggest factor anyway

if you have a go and cant achieve something you would like to, drop a comment and ill see what I can do
